title: Quantum Steering Geometry at High Energy Particle Colliders
authors: Juan J. Mejia Alvarez, Andrew J. Wildridge, Angelo Arisi, Juan M. Duarte-Quiros, Santosh Bhandari, Jingyan Li, Giulia Negro, Andreas W. Jung
abstract: We formulate collider observables based on quantum steering ellipsoids (QSEs) for reconstructed bipartite systems of spin-$1/2$ particles. A collider spin density matrix defines a two-qubit state, while its QSE gives the geometry of conditional states accessible through local measurements. This makes the ellipsoid a direct probe of the quantum properties of fundamental particles, encoding polarization, spin correlation anisotropy, accessible-state volume, and the orientation of the dominant correlation axes. Using top-quark pair production as a benchmark process, we show how QSE observables organize the Standard Model spin state, probe entanglement, steerability, and Bell-nonlocality criteria, and use an expected precision metric to assess sensitivity to non-local correlations in the boosted central region. We show that different dimension-six operators generate distinctive QSE deformations, and provide a geometric interpretation of quantum information observables in high-energy particle physics. Quantum steering geometry therefore provides a unified framework for particle collider tomography, quantum information diagnostics, and precision searches for physics beyond the Standard Model with applications spanning the HL--LHC and future lepton, muon, flavor, and electron-ion collider programs.
summary: This work introduces Quantum Steering Ellipsoids (QSEs) as a novel, geometrically rich set of observables for analyzing quantum states in high-energy particle collisions. By mapping the conditional state space onto an ellipsoid, the authors provide a unified diagnostic tool to test fundamental quantum principles like entanglement and non-locality. This framework offers a powerful method for precision searches for physics beyond the Standard Model at colliders like the HL-LHC.
main_problem: The paper formulates and utilizes Quantum Steering Ellipsoids (QSEs) as a novel class of observables to probe the quantum properties of fundamental particle interactions at high-energy colliders.
main_result: QSEs provide a unified, geometrically interpretable framework for particle collider tomography, allowing for the direct probing of entanglement, steerability, and non-local correlations beyond the Standard Model.
method: The QSE is derived by analyzing the geometric locus of conditional quantum states accessible through local measurements on a bipartite spin system, using the Fano representation for the density matrix.
model_or_system: The system is based on reconstructed bipartite states of spin-1/2 particles (two-qubit states) arising from high-energy particle collisions, benchmarked using top-quark pair production ($t ar{t}$).
key_observables: Quantum Steering Ellipsoids (QSEs), characterized by their center ($\vec{c}_{A|B}$) and shape matrix ($Q_{A|B}$); these probe polarization, spin correlation anisotropy, and accessible-state volume.
important_parameters: The analysis uses NLO QCD simulations and is sensitive to dimension-six operators, providing diagnostic power for physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM).
main_assumptions: The QSE construction relies on the narrow-width approximation, and practical measurements involve coarse-graining over finite solid-angle bins.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates an example of a QSE embedded in the Bloch sphere, showing its center and semi-axes.
paper_structure: The paper develops the mathematical formalism for QSEs from the spin density matrix, applies this framework to benchmark processes like $t ar{t}$ production, and demonstrates how the resulting geometric observables can diagnose quantum properties and constrain BSM physics.
why_interesting: The geometric interpretation of quantum information measures (like the QSE) provides a powerful, intuitive tool for analyzing complex quantum states, which is valuable for understanding the structure of quantum correlations in any physical system, including those modeled by Hamiltonians relevant to AMO physics.
